arms.predicted: Cold lookup throughput consistently above 4.5 GB/s with QD32 x 4 threads x 4 streams on 2 drives, matching iter-1 best achieved via single-object path modifications.
arms.observed: Cold lookup: 5.63 GB/s (seed 1), 5.55 GB/s (seed 2), avg 5.59 GB/s. P99 latency: 884.6 us (seed 1), 937.9 us (seed 2). Data integrity PASS (0 errors). Improvement: +47% over baseline avg (3.63 GB/s). Exceeds the 4.5 GB/s prediction.
arms.diagnostic_note: The improvement exceeds prediction (5.59 vs 4.5 GB/s target). However, h-ablation (QD64, 2 threads) outperforms h-main (5.99 vs 5.59 GB/s), suggesting 4 threads introduce actor poll-loop contention that slightly reduces throughput. The 4-stream expansion adds overhead (CUDA stream creation, rotation) without benefit because 2 streams already saturate the PCIe DMA bandwidth at these throughput levels.

arms.predicted: Cold lookup throughput above 4.0 GB/s but below h-main's result. Queue depth is the primary factor but fewer threads mean more sequential object processing.
arms.observed: Cold lookup: 5.96 GB/s (seed 1), 6.01 GB/s (seed 2), avg 5.99 GB/s. P99 latency: 875.5 us (seed 1), 869.9 us (seed 2). Data integrity PASS (0 errors). OUTPERFORMS h-main by 7% (5.99 vs 5.59 GB/s).
arms.diagnostic_note: Direction partially wrong: predicted ablation < h-main, but observed ablation > h-main. The throughput IS above 4.0 GB/s (confirmed), but the ordering is reversed. QD64 per thread with 2 threads is the optimal configuration. Adding more threads (4) actually hurts because: (1) the single-threaded NVMe actor poll loop becomes saturated processing 4 command channels vs 2, (2) CUDA stream creation/destruction overhead is doubled, (3) 2 threads × QD64 = aggregate QD128 already saturates the NVMe controller without the contention of 4 threads competing for actor attention.

arms.predicted: Cold lookup above 3.0 GB/s single-drive baseline without NVMe submission failures, because 128 KiB chunks with QD32 per thread require only 4 MiB of scatter-gather entries per thread.
arms.observed: Cold lookup: 3.89 GB/s (seed 1, 3 ENOMEM errors), 3.81 GB/s (seed 2, 2 ENOMEM errors). P99 latency: 1258.4 us (seed 1), 1299.3 us (seed 2). Data integrity: PARTIAL FAIL (sporadic rc=-12 ENOMEM on NVMe submit). Throughput on successful iterations is above 3.0 GB/s prediction but errors violate the 'without NVMe submission failures' criterion.
arms.diagnostic_note: Throughput criterion met (3.85 GB/s avg > 3.0 GB/s target) but ENOMEM errors confirm RP-3 extends to 128 KiB chunks at aggregate QD128 on a single controller. With 4 threads × QD32 = 128 max pending commands, plus each command needing scatter-gather entries, the single controller's queue pair depth-256 is sufficient but the NVMe request tracker or scatter-gather pool is exhausted during burst submission. The errors are sporadic (2-3 per 10 iterations), not fatal, but violate hard data integrity constraints.

discrepancy_analysis: The primary surprise is that h-ablation (QD64, 2 threads, 2 streams) outperforms h-main (QD32, 4 threads, 4 streams) by 7%. This refutes the hypothesis that more threads provide additional benefit beyond queue depth. The mechanism is that 2 threads × QD64 saturates the NVMe controller equivalently to 4 × QD32 (both aggregate to QD128) but with less actor poll-loop contention. The actor is single-threaded (processes all channels) and handles 2 channels more efficiently than 4. The h-robustness arm confirms that RP-3 (ENOMEM at deep aggregate QD) applies to 128 KiB chunks when all traffic hits one controller, not just 512 KiB. The ENOMEM boundary appears to be around aggregate QD96-128 per controller.
